newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Rabobank NZ sees measured growth path.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Rabobank NZ sees measured growth path.

text.p: Rabobank Group's New Zealand General Manager Jaap Klep said on Monday the branch would continue along a measured growth path in its chosen field of top tier agribusiness lending.
"We continue to build on our rural side and we are building up our corporate side," Klep said in an interview. "But we are not here to drive around in fast Ferraris," he said.
Rabobank is at present involved in the top end of the farm lending market and lends to large agricultural corporates.
The Netherlands-based Rabobank is looking to tap the mid-sized agricultural corporate, Klep said.

Rabobank took over Primary Industry Bank of Australia (PIBA) in 1994. PIBA had been operating as a farm lender in New Zealand since 1989 but Rabobank formally opened its doors as a branch on receiving a New Zealand banking licence in August.
The move was designed to reflect the international nature of Rabobank but PIBA would remain as a brand name, he said.
In farm lending, Klep said the bank was looking at setting up more loan offices outside its existing areas of Auckland, Christchurch, Dunedin and Palmerston North.
Klep agreed with other commentators that New Zealand is over-banked, but fully recognised why so many are here and why others were waiting in the wings.

"New Zealand has now been proven to have a good, sustainable economy and therefore I think you will see foreign investments coming into New Zealand. When that is the case, the banks have always tried to tag along."

While farmers were feeling the pinch from high New Zealand dollar and low beef and wool prices, the good operators would come through it. "They are all waiting for turn in the cycle. It will come," he said.
Over the longer term, Rabobank had taken the positive view on New Zealand agriculture.
"We have taken a view that there is an ability to be a low cost producer. As long as they can keep doing that, then I think the've got a magnificant future."
Klep said expects to see more consolidation in farming, resulting in larger units.
With much of New Zealand's landscape being taken up with afforestation, Rabobank was looking at becoming involved but does not see itself as a front runner.
Rabobank's New Zealand book consists of NZ$220 million in rural loans and $250 million in corporate and export sectors.
